analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal oil and gas leases held by companies the FTC finds conspired with OPEC to rig oil prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never left committee: introduced in July 2024 with one cosponsor, it was referred to the Senate Energy Committee and received no hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: If the Federal Trade Commission issued a final order finding that a company holding a federal oil and gas lease worked with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to illegally manipulate oil or gas prices, the Interior Department would have to cancel that company's federal leases, refuse to renew them, and bar the company from bidding on new federal leases. The bill was introduced by Senator Markey, referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee, and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy gasoline and heating fuel, if price manipulation by leaseholders colluding with foreign oil producers is found and deterred, and taxpayers who own the federal mineral estate, which would no longer be leased to companies found to have broken antitrust law. The benefit is indirect and conditional: it only applies after an actual FTC enforcement order.

how_it_helps.text: The bill would strip federal oil and gas leases from any company the FTC formally finds coordinated with an OPEC or OPEC-plus country to manipulate oil or gas prices in violation of antitrust law, and would permanently bar that company from bidding on new federal leases.

It targets the specific situation consumer advocates have long flagged: American oil producers coordinating output and pricing with the foreign cartel that controls a large share of world oil supply, which raises prices for ordinary drivers and households.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies: any leaseholder the FTC finds violated antitrust law by coordinating with OPEC countries would lose its federal leases and its ability to bid on new ones, and the industry as a whole would face a new enforcement risk on its federal lease portfolio.

drawbacks.text: The bill's trigger is narrow and untested: it applies only after the FTC issues a final order finding that a specific leaseholder coordinated with a named list of OPEC and OPEC-plus countries to manipulate prices. No such order exists, so the bill's real-world effect would hinge entirely on future enforcement the FTC might never undertake.

The cancellation duty is hedged as applying only 'to the extent allowable by law', an acknowledgment that canceling existing leases — which companies paid for and hold under contract — could raise legal questions about compensation and due process that the bill does not resolve.

Supporters would have to acknowledge that canceling a handful of leases would do little on its own to lower pump prices, since domestic prices are set in a global market and the bill does nothing about OPEC's own production decisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a targeted penalty, not a price-control program: it imposes a real consequence (lease cancellation and a bidding ban) only on companies formally found to have broken antitrust law in league with a foreign cartel, so the cost to compliant companies is minimal. Its weakness is the opposite of overreach — it is so conditional on an FTC finding that its practical effect would likely have been small, and its legal footing for voiding existing leases is untested.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee without a hearing or vote until the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Markey introduced the bill on July 25, 2024, in the final months of the 118th Congress, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.
One Democratic senator cosponsored the bill; no other members of either party signed on.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas companies holding federal leases are better off: they face no risk of having leases canceled or being barred from future bidding, and the industry avoids a new enforcement precedent tying federal leases to antitrust violations involving OPEC.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action on it — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; with no committee action, it never became eligible for a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats supported the bill — Markey and a single Democratic cosponsor — and no Republican signed on or acted to advance it before it died in committee.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies with federal leases
industries.note: If passed, the bill would let the government cancel the federal leases of any company the FTC finds conspired with OPEC countries to rig prices, and would ban it from future lease sales. The industry's interest in keeping its lease portfolio and bidding rights runs against consumers who absorb artificially high prices.
The bill would add an enforcement condition to the federal leasing program, tying continued access to public minerals to lawful market behavior. It does not restrict leasing generally.
